How to Open HTML Files

A lot of what the AI tools produce - reports, digests, checklists, dashboards - comes as an .html file. Here is how to open one and see it the way it's meant to look.
For Team Members

An HTML file is just a web page saved to your computer. It ends in .html. You don't need internet for it and you don't need any special software - your web browser already opens it.

The short version: download the file, then double-click it - or drag it onto a Google Chrome window. It opens like any web page.

Open it in 3 steps

1
Download the file
Save it somewhere you'll find it again - your Downloads folder or Desktop is fine. If it came as an attachment or a link, choose Download (not "open in a new tab," which may just show the raw code).
2
Double-click it
It should open in your default browser automatically. If it opens as plain code or in the wrong app, right-click the file → Open with → Google Chrome.
3
Read it like a web page
Scroll, click buttons, expand sections - it behaves like any site. Nothing is sent anywhere; the file lives on your computer.

Use Google Chrome

Any browser will open an HTML file - Edge, Firefox, Safari - so if you're in a pinch, use what you have. But we standardize on Google Chrome at School Tech, and some of what we build uses features that only render fully in Chrome.

Heads-up: open our files in Chrome to get the full effect. In Edge or another browser, most of it still works, but you may see missing pieces or things that don't behave the way they should. When something looks broken, re-open it in Chrome before assuming the file is wrong.

To make Chrome your default so double-clicking always uses it: Chrome menu (⋮) → Settings → Default browser → Make default. Or on Windows: Settings → Apps → Default apps and set Chrome for web pages.

Common snags

It opened as a wall of code. You're seeing the raw HTML, not the page. Right-click the file → Open with → Google Chrome.
It won't open / opens in a text editor. The file is set to open in the wrong app. Right-click → Open with → Choose another app → pick Google Chrome and check "always use this app."
You only see a download link, never the page. Some email and chat tools preview the code instead of rendering it. Download the file first, then open the downloaded copy.
That's it. Download → double-click (or drag into Chrome) → read. When in doubt, Chrome.
